tldr: We show that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can be trained to directly control and generalize to real robots natively through reinforcement learning (RL) entirely in simulation—without any human demonstrations, specialized tools, or harnesses.
hero_caption: Comparison between a computer-use agent (CUA) and the robot-use agent (RUA) in this work. Much like a CUA determines click positions from screenshots, the RUA takes camera images and arm states, reasons through a chain of thought, and outputs the next end-effector pose to control the robot directly.
overview:
Robot-use agents (RUAs), where a vision-language model (VLM) directly controls a robot, have emerged as a promising approach for general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, strong performance has so far been achieved only by frontier proprietary models like GPT-6 Astra, whereas open-weight models have remained substantially less capable or forced to rely on external harnesses (auxiliary tools) such as object detectors and skill libraries.

To bridge this gap, the authors looked at how frontier models acquire computer use (CUAs). They hypothesized that reasoning models could natively learn "how to use a robot" purely through multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, without any human demonstrations. To make this possible, they built a Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics (PEAR)—a dedicated infrastructure designed to efficiently scale training over long reasoning traces and trajectories—and trained an open-weight 27B model.

Evaluation shows that the model, trained solely with sparse binary rewards (task success or failure) in simulation, boosted its success rate on the LIBERO benchmark from 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching frontier models at their maximum reasoning effort. Furthermore, it demonstrated strong robustness to novel instructions and rearranged objects, achieving a 60% success rate in zero-shot transfer to a real dual-arm YAM robot. This work clearly highlights robot-use reinforcement learning as a promising component of foundation-model post-training.
contributions: Demonstrated that an open-weight 27B reasoning model can acquire real-robot control capabilities purely through reinforcement learning in simulation, without human demonstrations or external tools (harnesses).
Developed PEAR, a training infrastructure designed to efficiently scale multi-turn reinforcement learning with long context windows.
Showed that a model trained purely in simulation achieves strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks, an unseen simulator, and an unseen real dual-arm robot.
Confirmed that acquiring robot-use capabilities causes no measurable degradation on nine general foundation-model benchmarks spanning math, coding, and reasoning.

sections.heading: Introduction: Bringing "robot use" from proprietary frontier models to open models
sections.summary: While RUAs that directly control robots exhibit strong generalization, they have previously succeeded only with commercial frontier models such as GPT-6 Astra. Mirroring the training pipeline of CUAs, this work opens a new path by training an open-weight reasoning model purely through simulation RL to drive real robots.
sections.details:
In recent years, robot-use agents (RUAs)—where vision-language models (VLMs) reason over camera images and directly output target end-effector poses to control a robot—have emerged as a promising direction. The concept mirrors computer-use agents (CUAs), which view computer screens to generate clicks and keystrokes.

So far, RUAs powered by cutting-edge commercial models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.2 have shown remarkable generalization. In contrast, conventional vision-language-action (VLA) models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstrations struggle heavily when faced with novel goals or unseen instructions. The primary strength of frontier RUAs appears to stem from their spatial reasoning capabilities via chain-of-thought (CoT).

However, prior attempts to replicate this with open-weight models yielded extremely low success rates. Previous works attempted to compensate by attaching external "harnesses"—such as object detectors (e.g., SAM 3) or motion primitive libraries. Unfortunately, these restrict the action space and strip away the model's inherent flexibility.

The authors therefore hypothesized: "If CUAs are trained via reinforcement learning, RUAs should also be able to learn natively from scratch via RL in simulation." This spurred their pursuit of robot-use reinforcement learning (RURL)—teaching a model to use robots through trial and error and its own reasoning, without a single demonstration.

sections.heading: Related Work: Moving beyond external tools toward a new wave of RL
sections.summary: While conventional RUA research for open models relies heavily on external harnesses, this work adopts pure reinforcement learning without external tools. It translates the successful recipe of CUAs—which master web and OS navigation via multi-turn RL—into the realm of robotics.
sections.details:
Related work broadly falls into two areas: RUA system architectures and reinforcement learning for agents.

The first area is harness design for robot-use agents (RUAs). To compensate for the limitations of open models, many studies (such as ORA, ASPIRE, and Harness VLA) have built frameworks equipped with external perception tools, motion primitives, or memory modules. Recent efforts have begun training open models with RL inside such harnesses. In contrast, this work fundamentally diverges by "completely eliminating harnesses." The goal is for the model itself to locate target objects directly from images, recognize mistakes, and derive the next action on its own.

The second area is the advancement of multi-turn reinforcement learning in computer-use agents (CUAs). In environments like OSWorld and WebArena, open agents such as UI-TARS-2 and DigiRL have learned long-horizon reasoning and execution through RL. Furthermore, RL with verifiable rewards has proven highly effective for expanding reasoning processes autonomously, suffering far less catastrophic forgetting of pre-existing skills than SFT while generalizing better. This study directly transfers this CUA reinforcement learning recipe to simulated robot manipulation.

sections.heading: Method: How robot reinforcement learning works without tools or demonstrations
sections.summary: By unifying robot control into an interaction protocol identical to CUAs, RL is conducted on the dedicated PEAR infrastructure using only binary success/failure rewards (0 or 1). Because initial success rates are near zero, a three-stage curriculum based on task difficulty is adopted.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Robot-Use Agent Protocol
The interaction between the model and the environment is remarkably simple. At each turn, the model receives multi-view camera images and the current arm state, reasons via CoT, and outputs the next end-effector pose displacement (in cm and radians) formatted in JSON. External inverse kinematics (IK) and low-level controllers then convert this pose into joint angles to actuate the robot.

Crucially, no visual perception tools or motion planners are involved. The model itself determines where objects are in the images, how to reach with the arm, and whether to retry after a mistake. Moreover, because the action interface is standardized on pose commands, the exact same framework operates across a single-arm Franka in simulation, a dual-arm ARX in simulation, or a real dual-arm YAM simply by updating the robot description in the prompt.

### 3.2 Large-Scale RL Infrastructure: PEAR
To reliably execute reinforcement learning over long context windows, the authors built PEAR (Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics). Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) serves as the core algorithm, generating $G$ episodes in parallel from the same task and initial state to compute relative advantages within the group.

The reward $R(\tau)$ is strictly binary—1 if the task is completed, 0 otherwise. No intermediate human-engineered step rewards are provided. The whole-episode advantage is distributed uniformly across all generated tokens, including reasoning tokens, to update the policy. Asynchronous policy drift is mitigated via score-centering corrections, while KV caching efficiency is maintained at an exceptionally high hit rate by utilizing LMCache for CPU offloading.

### 3.3 Curriculum Learning
When training purely with binary rewards, tasks where the initial model never succeeds yield zero learning signal (zero gradient). The base model's initial success rate was only about 2% on basic LIBERO tasks and 0.4% on long-horizon tasks.

To address this, training begins on three LIBERO suites (Goal, Spatial, Object) where non-zero success signals exist. Once fundamental spatial manipulation is acquired, the curriculum expands to all four suites including the long-horizon LIBERO-Long, and finally introduces dual-arm manipulation tasks in RoboDojo in a staged manner.

captions.F2: The execution flow of a single turn in robot operation. The model takes camera images and the current arm state, produces a chain-of-thought reasoning trace, and outputs the target end-effector pose. The IK and controller drive the arm, and the resulting observation is appended to the context for the next step of reasoning.

sections.heading: Results: Approaching frontier models in generalization and zero-shot real-world transfer
sections.summary: LIBERO success rates surged from an initial 1.6% to 74.4%, approaching GPT-6 Astra. The model demonstrated strong robustness to unseen task perturbations, zero-shot transfer across simulators and robots, and achieved a 60% success rate on a real dual-arm robot.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Training Performance on LIBERO
The base model (Qwen3.8-27B) started with a meager 1.6% success rate, but improved rapidly as RL training progressed, ultimately reaching 74.4%. This significantly outperforms GPT-6.1 Sol (48.1%) and GPT-6 Astra (49.3%) under medium reasoning effort, and nears their performance at maximum reasoning effort (76.2% for GPT-6.1 Sol and 80.6% for GPT-6 Astra). Achieving this level purely through reinforcement learning without any imitation learning is a striking result.

### 4.2 Robustness and Instruction Following
A comparison with $\pi_{0.5}$, a state-of-the-art VLA model fine-tuned on demonstrations, revealed stark differences in generalization. On LIBERO-Plus, which alters visual appearances, both models suffered only modest drops of around 11 to 12 points. However, on LIBERO-Pro, which modifies instructions and goals, the results diverged dramatically.

When assigned a different task within a familiar scene, $\pi_{0.5}$ blindly repeated memorized demonstration trajectories, suffering a catastrophic 96.2-point collapse in success rate from 96.9% down to 0.75%. In contrast, the RL-trained model comprehended the instruction semantically and flexibly adjusted its actions, retaining a 57.4% success rate. A similar resilience was observed when initial object locations were swapped, illustrating the strong instruction-following capabilities inherent to reasoning models.

### 4.3 Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Tasks and Robots
Even before training on LIBERO-Long (at step 148), the model solved LIBERO-Long tasks with a 39.0% success rate (compared to 0.4% for the base model). Furthermore, when a model trained solely on single-arm Franka tasks in LIBERO was evaluated in RoboDojo on a dual-arm ARX robot, it recorded a 39.9% success rate on general_pickup and 17.0% on align_blocks. On the unseen tabletop benchmark RoboLab-120, it achieved 37.3%, outperforming other policies on the leaderboard (such as $\pi_{0.5}$ at 28.0%).

### 4.4 Zero-Shot Transfer to Real Dual-Arm YAM and Reasoning Tasks
Despite never seeing real-robot data during training, the final model achieved an 18/30 (60%) success rate in real dual-arm YAM evaluations, compared to 0% for the base model. Even the checkpoint trained solely on LIBERO reached a 23% success rate.

Furthermore, the model was tested on "reasoning tasks" entirely absent from training data. In tasks such as drawing a line reproduction of Van Gogh's *The Starry Night* on a whiteboard, or identifying an alkaline solution by selecting and pouring phenolphthalein rather than ethanol or iodine, the model seamlessly combined the foundational commonsense of the base model with physical robot manipulation.

### 4.5 Retention of General Capabilities and Thinking Time
Undergoing reinforcement learning specialized for robot use caused zero degradation across nine standard benchmarks, including mathematics (AIME 2026: 98.5), scientific reasoning (GPQA Diamond: 89.7), and coding (LiveCodeBench: 88.4). This aligns with prior observations that RL post-training is less prone to catastrophic forgetting.

captions.F7: Evaluation results on the real dual-arm YAM robot. Despite using no real-world training data, the model succeeded in 12/20 object grasping trials (a) and 6/10 block alignment trials using a set square (b). In (c), the robot autonomously performed complex reasoning tasks absent from training, such as sketching a painting and selecting the correct reagent in a chemistry experiment.

sections.heading: Limitations: Long thinking times and headroom for scaling
sections.summary: Key limitations include slow operation due to lengthy reasoning traces, high turn counts from single-pose action outputs, and a restricted number of training tasks dictated by computational constraints.
sections.details:
Despite these promising results, several clear limitations remain.

First is inference latency (thinking time). Because the model conducts elaborate chain-of-thought reasoning before acting, each turn takes an average of approximately 4.3 seconds. In some cases, reasoning traces reached 32k tokens, taking over 30 seconds for a single motion. Because no length penalty was enforced during RL, future work must explore ways to encourage concise thinking without hurting task success.

Second is the absence of action chunking: the model outputs only a single target pose per turn. Consequently, complex behaviors must be broken down into many individual turns, increasing the overall step count. Additionally, whether the arm reaches the designated pose accurately depends entirely on the tracking performance of the external low-level controller.

Third is training scale. Constrained by GPU compute, simulation training was limited to two environments and a small set of tasks. Scaling up training across broader, more diverse simulator environments and starting from stronger foundation models leaves substantial room for future gains.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Integrating robot use into foundation-model post-training
sections.summary: This work demonstrates that open reasoning models can acquire sophisticated real-world robot control purely through simulation RL without demonstrations or external tools, establishing a new paradigm that incorporates robot RL into post-training pipelines.
sections.details:
This paper validates that general-purpose reasoning models can natively operate robots without relying on external tools, achieved entirely through reinforcement learning in simulation.

Starting from a base model with near-zero initial success, pairing a suitable curriculum with the multi-turn RL engine PEAR unlocked a 74.4% success rate on LIBERO—approaching frontier proprietary models—and enabled direct zero-shot transfer to unseen robots and real environments. Importantly, this physical control ability was added without sacrificing any of the model's pre-existing reasoning or coding strengths.

Historically, the biggest bottleneck in robotic learning has been collecting high-quality real-world teleoperation or demonstration data. This research showcases a highly scalable alternative: taking foundation models made intelligent on web-scale data and grounding them with embodiment through autonomous reinforcement learning in simulation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Behind the scenes of PEAR, the large-scale agent RL infrastructure
sections.summary: To support multi-turn RL over massive token sequences, PEAR integrates FSDP, sequence parallelism, LMCache, and score-centering corrections. The appendix also details failure analyses, including context window exhaustion.
sections.details:
### Infrastructure Architecture and Distributed Training
PEAR (Post-training Engine for Agentic Robotics) was built on top of the veRL reinforcement learning framework and the LMCache engine. It is optimized for clusters of cutting-edge GPUs including H100, H200, and GB300, consuming roughly 50,000 H100-equivalent GPU hours across training.

During training, an average episode contains approximately 94k tokens across 19.7 turns and 39 to 59 images. To handle such ultra-long sequences, PEAR combines Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), Sequence Parallelism (SP), and gradient checkpointing. On H100 nodes, LMCache offloads prefix KV caches to host CPU memory, sustaining a cache hit rate above 95%.

### Failure Mode Analysis
Analyzing real-robot failures revealed that the base model timed out by exceeding the 25-turn limit in 25 out of 30 trials. In contrast, the 12 failures of the final model broke down into: 6 turn limit timeouts, 3 misaligned blocks, 2 knocked-over objects, and 1 rolled-off tennis ball. Failures clustered around objects with tricky physical dynamics, such as tippable air pumps or grasping brushes.

Across the full RoboDojo benchmark (540 episodes), 68.5% of all failures stemmed from the model exhausting its maximum context window of 256k tokens. This highlights the crucial need for models with even longer contexts or mechanisms to effectively compress and summarize interaction histories.

takeaways: Reasoning models can master real-robot manipulation skills purely through reinforcement learning in simulation, without requiring a single human demonstration.

By adopting a native setup free of external perception tools or motion libraries (harnesses), the model exhibits far greater robustness and instruction following under task modifications than imitation-based VLA models.
Post-training on robot tasks causes no degradation in foundation model benchmarks like math, coding, or reasoning, suggesting robot RL can become a standard post-training stage.

Current challenges lie in inference latency (several to tens of seconds per step) and heavy context window consumption, highlighting concise reasoning and action chunking as critical future research directions.
limitations: Lengthy chain-of-thought traces incur several seconds or more of inference latency per action, making the system unsuitable for high-speed or real-time reactive control.
Actions are restricted to a single target end-effector pose per turn; lacking action chunking to predict continuous trajectories, tasks require many turns to execute.
Due to computational constraints, training was limited to two simulated environments and a modest task suite; scaling up to cover truly diverse everyday tasks remains future work.
